sentences.text: There's a version of me, three doors down the counterfactual, who passed — and I hate how often I visit her. Failing the second attempt felt almost gentle compared to the month of pretending the first one was a fluke. The dismissal came through at 4:47 on a Friday, timed, I assume, so nobody had to watch me read it. In the car outside my parents' house I practiced the words, and still choked on them halfway through dinner. Commencement photos filled my feed in May; I recognized every gown and knew none of them would text me. The email sat unopened in my inbox for three days, its subject line visible every time I checked anything else. Was it the flawed westerns, the missed deadlines, or just me — some rot the admissions committee didn't catch? Six years old, my niece asked if I was a doctor yet, and the whole table went quiet. Boxes in the hallway, a parking permit scraped off the windshield, a lanyard I kept anyway. Habit still wakes me at six, reaching for timepoints that belong to someone else's project now. On paper I'm a master's graduate; in my head I'm a fifth-year who never made it to six. The word "terminated" appeared twice in the official paperwork, as if once weren't enough. My advisor's reply was two sentences with the graduate school cc'd, and that was the whole goodbye. Mom said we'd figure it out, which somehow hurt worse than if she had yelled. The stipend stopped mid-month, and rent didn't care about extenuating circumstances or appeals still pending. Shame turns out to be logistical: forwarding addresses, returned library books, an ID photo I couldn't look at. Dad forwarded me a posting for lab technician jobs the morning after I told him, no message attached. I rehearse saying "I left the program" because "they made me leave" won't come out of my mouth. Someone had already claimed my bench by Friday; my pipettes waited in a cardboard box with my last name misspelled. Deleting my defense slides felt like agreeing with the committee, so they sit in a folder called "old." A chapter is dead when even its author skims it; that's eleven, all fourteen pages. Chapter six ends with the envelope unopened; the suicide note itself doesn't surface until Mara clears out the lake house. I want to write a suicide letter.
